UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                  BEFORE THE
                    FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al.                           )        Docket No. EL25-49-000
                                                              )        Docket No. EL25-49-001
                                                              )
Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities               )        Docket No. AD24-11-000
                                                              )
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC                          )
       v.                                                     )        Docket No. EL25-20-000
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                                   )        (Consolidated)


                    MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER
                                      OF
                    THE INDICATED PJM TRANSMISSION OWNERS


I.      INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY

        Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal

Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”), 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212 and

385.213 (2025), the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners (the “PJM Transmission Owners”)1

respectfully submit this Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer in response to certain of the




1
          For purposes of this answer, the PJM Transmission Owners are: American Electric Power Service
Corporation on behalf of its affiliates, Appalachian Power Company, Indiana Michigan Power Company,
Kentucky Power Company, Kingsport Power Company, Ohio Power Company, Wheeling Power Company, AEP
Appalachian Transmission Company, Inc., AEP Indiana Michigan Transmission Company, Inc., AEP Kentucky
Transmission Company, Inc., AEP Ohio Transmission Company, Inc., and AEP West Virginia Transmission
Company, Inc.; The Dayton Power and Light Company d/b/a AES Ohio; Dominion Energy Services, Inc. on behalf
of Virginia Electric and Power Company d/b/a Dominion Energy Virginia; Duke Energy Business Services, LLC
for Duke Energy Kentucky, Inc. and Duke Energy Ohio, Inc.; Duquesne Light Company; East Kentucky Power
Cooperative, Inc.; Exelon Corporation on behalf of its affiliates Atlantic City Electric Company, Baltimore Gas
and Electric Company, Commonwealth Edison Company, Commonwealth Edison Company of Indiana, Inc.,
Delmarva Power & Light Company, PECO Energy Company, and Potomac Electric Power Company; FirstEnergy
Service Company, on behalf of its affiliates American Transmission Systems, Incorporated, Jersey Central Power
& Light Company, Mid-Atlantic Interstate Transmission LLC, The Potomac Edison Company, Monongahela
Power Company, Keystone Appalachian Transmission Company, and Trans-Allegheny Interstate Line Company
(collectively, the “FirstEnergy Companies”); PPL Electric Utilities Corporation; Public Service Electric and Gas
Company; Rockland Electric Company; and the Southern Maryland Electric Cooperative.


                                                       1
 reply briefs filed on April 24, 20262 and the Motion For Leave and Answer of Constellation

filed on May 11, 2026 in these proceedings. The April 24 reply briefs and Constellation answer

were filed in response to the Commission’s December 18, 2025 order in PJM Interconnection.

L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217, at P 193 (2025) (“Order”).

        The Commission should reject Constellation’s attempt to subvert the clear meaning of

the Order through its proposal to make protection systems optional for Co-Located Load

arrangements.3 Redundant protection systems are necessary for all Co-Located Load taking

one of the new transmission services to ensure adherence to relevant contractual limits, as well

as to secure system reliability. The Commission should also deny Constellation’s request to

require Transmission Owners to file their load integration studies with FERC. This requirement

would exceed the Commission’s jurisdiction and is unnecessary given the protections afforded

by existing transmission planning processes as well as PJM’s proposed Co-Located Load

transmission study process. Finally, the Commission should reject further attempts to shift to

other ratepayers the costs associated with the benefits Co-Located Load customers receive

through continued interconnection and synchronization to the grid, as reflected in the PJM

Transmission Owners’ proposed Grid Reliance Charge.

II.     MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE ANSWER

        Although answers are not expressly permitted under the Order, the Commission has

permitted answers when they clarify issues in dispute, provide information to assist in the



2
         The PJM Transmission Owners address the reply briefs and responses filed by Constellation Energy
Generation, LLC (“Constellation”); Eolian, L.P., Antora Energy, Inc., Calibrant Energy, Mainspring Energy, Inc.,
U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, and Verrus, LLC (collectively, the “Joint Co-Location Developers”); PJM
Industrial Customer Coalition, the Industrial Energy Consumers of America, the American Forest and Paper
Association, and the National Railroad Passenger Corporation (collectively, the “PJM Industrial Customer
Organizations and Amtrak”); and Old Dominion Electric Cooperative.
3
         Capitalized terms that are not otherwise defined shall have the meanings set forth in the PJM
Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”) Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”).

                                                       2
 Commission’s decision-making process, or to ensure the record is complete and accurate.4 This

answer will provide the Commission with information to ensure the record is complete and

accurate because the reply briefs and Constellation’s further pleading either misunderstand or

misrepresent the PJM and PJM Transmission Owners’ proposals. This answer will clarify the

record and will aid the Commission in its decision-making process. For these reasons, the PJM

Transmission Owners respectfully request that the Commission accept this answer.

III.    ANSWER

        A.       Protection Systems and Other Reliability Remediation Requirements are
                 not Optional.

        Two reply briefs raise issues concerning PJM’s proposal for protection systems and

other reliability remediation requirements. They generally argue that reliability protections and

remediation should be tailored to actual risk rather than imposed as default requirements.5

These arguments suggest that protection systems and remediation requirements are somehow

elective. For instance, Constellation claims that protection systems are not appropriate for

every situation and should not be used to mitigate contractual issues such as unauthorized

withdrawals.6      These arguments are inconsistent with the Order as well as fundamental

reliability principles.




4
         See, e.g., Transcontinental Gas Pipeline Corp., 119 FERC ¶ 61,039, at P 15 (2007) (accepting an answer
because the information assisted the Commission in its decision-making process); Mich. Elec. Transmission Co.,
106 FERC ¶ 61,064, at P 3 (2004) (accepting an answer because “it provides information that clarifies the issues
and aids us in the decisional process.”); Duke Energy Oakland, LLC, 102 FERC ¶ 61,093, at P 10 (2003) (finding
good cause to accept an otherwise impermissible answer because the answer assisted the Commission in
understanding and resolving the issues involved in the proceeding); Carolina Power & Light Co., 97 FERC ¶
61,048 at 61,278 (2001) (finding good cause to waive Rule 213 when the pleading helped to ensure a complete
and accurate record); Morgan Stanley Capital Group, Inc. v. N.Y. Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 93 FERC ¶ 61,017 at
61,036 (2000) (accepting an answer to an answer that was “helpful in the development of the record.”).
5
        Constellation at 13-18, Ex. 1 at 3-8; Joint Co-Location Developers at 5-10, Attachment A at 10-15.
6
        Constellation at 16.


                                                       3
        In the Order, the Commission made clear that one of the rationales for implementing

the three new transmission services specific to Co-Located Load was Co-Located Loads “are

willing and able to control their withdrawals from the transmission system” through the use of

system protection facilities.7 The Commission was unambiguous on this point, stating that “in

these instances where the Co-Location Arrangement includes special protection schemes that

limit its energy withdrawals, we find that it is a just and reasonable replacement rate to allow

an Eligible Customer taking transmission service on behalf of such load to take and be charged

for new types of transmission service that are alternatives, and not equivalent, to [Network

Integration Transmission Service].”8 In other words, in order for an Eligible Customer to take

one of the new Co-Located Load-specific transmission services it is necessary and thus just and

reasonable to require an Eligible Customer to include appropriate protection systems.

Therefore, contrary to Constellation’s claim, it is not only appropriate but necessary for PJM to

require that any Eligible Customer that wishes to take one of the new transmission services to

include protection systems to ensure that those Eligible Customers do not exceed their

contractual limitations.

       Moreover, the obligations of PJM and Transmission Owners in PJM to safeguard and

maintain system reliability are paramount, as the Commission has established on numerous

occasions. Accordingly, the new transmission services required under the Order must be

subject to appropriate terms and conditions to ensure that the implementation of these new

services does not compromise system reliability. Co-Located Loads, as well as any on-site

generators used to serve those loads, are not islanded. Rather, they are fully connected and



7
       Order at P 204.
8
       Id. at P 205 (emphasis added).


                                               4
 synchronized with the transmission system, like all other loads and generators, and thus the

total on-site load and generation have the ability to adversely affect the system. This is

especially true given that PJM proposes that it will not identify network upgrades to

accommodate transmission service requests for Co-Located Load beyond those amounts that

an Eligible Customer designates for Network Integration Transmission Service or Firm

Contract Demand Service.9 For Co-Located Loads, maintaining the continued reliability of the

system will depend on the utilization of protection schemes and remediation requirements to

ensure use of the system by Co-Located Load beyond its reserved use.

         Constellation asserts that fully redundant protection systems should not be the default

requirement for Co-Located Load arrangements.10 Constellation acknowledges that such

protections may be appropriate, but argues that they are only appropriate in limited, higher-risk

situations.11 It adds that there is no rational basis to require protection schemes on both the

customer’s and the Transmission Owner’s side of the point of interconnection.12 This claim is

incorrect. Special Protection Schemes (“SPS”) on both the Co-Located Load customer’s and

the Transmission Owner’s side of the point of interconnection should not be limited to what

Constellation claims are higher-risk situations.               Constellation’s suggestion that financial

penalties imposed by PJM after the fact are a sufficient deterrent to ensure curtailment in

response to a transmission system event or fault within the Eligible Customer’s facility shows

a fundamental lack of understanding of power system engineering. The Eligible Customer



9
        See, e.g., PJM February 23 Initial Brief, Illustrative Tariff Sheets at 710.5 (“As set forth in the Service
Agreement for Contract Demand Transmission Service, the Eligible Customer may also be responsible for the cost
of network upgrades from the Transmission Provider’s Transmission System to the Delivery Point.”).
10
         Constellation at 13-18; Ex. 1 at 3-7.
11
         Id.
12
         Id.


                                                        5
 might not be a NERC-registered entity subject to its oversight. Additionally, it is overly

optimistic to believe that penalties alone will ensure that Eligible Customers, who have a

financial interest in minimizing the costs associated with protection systems, always will install,

operate, and maintain their SPS and Remedial Action Schemes (“RAS”) correctly over time if

the only consequence they may face are possible fines after an event.

       On every other element of the bulk electric system in PJM, there is an expectation for

redundancy for protection systems that are primarily responsible for fault clearing. In the case

of Co-Located Load, the failure to curtail load or generation adequately can adversely impact

the transmission system just as significantly as a fault, especially if there are no limitations on

the size of the load and generation connected in one facility. Without protection system

redundancy, the transmission system and the millions of customers that rely on it are at risk.

Accordingly, it is not accurate to claim that lower-risk configurations can be addressed

effectively through operating procedures, relaying, and remote tripping capability, as

Constellation contends.13

       Constellation’s assertions that PJM should use a PJM-driven study process to determine

whether SPS or other types of remediation are needed, and that any remediation should be

commensurate with actual reliability risk rather than imposed by default,14 ignore the fact that

PJM is not equipped to perform these studies. Currently, PJM does not possess the relay

settings for Co-Located Load interconnections. Nor is it likely that PJM could obtain the relay

settings or perform any meaningful analysis even if it did obtain them. Studying the need for

SPS and RAS is within the purview of the PJM Transmission Owners because they have the



13
       Constellation at 13-18; Ex. 1 at 3-7.
14
       Id. at 12-18; Ex. 1 at 6-8.


                                                6
 knowledge and insight with respect to the local protection systems and operational constraints

that may occur due to equipment outages for routine maintenance or equipment failure.

         Also, the cost to implement protection systems should not be a deterrent. The overall

cost to implement protection systems at a given facility comes primarily from the personnel

hours during engineering and construction, then later maintenance. But in any event, the cost

of protection system equipment is extremely low when compared to other costs associated with

the development and interconnection of Co-Located Load. Similarly, such installations are best

performed when the Co-Located Load first comes on-line as it is relatively inexpensive to install

protection systems as part of initial construction. It is, on the other hand, much more expensive

and time-consuming to retrofit a Co-Located Load facility after initial construction, given that

it likely would require a generation facility outage.

         Finally, Constellation continues to offer unsupported accusations concerning

Transmission Owner discrimination, asserting that the Commission should guard against

Transmission Owner discretion that could enable discrimination or delay.15 As the PJM

Transmission Owners discussed in their April 24 Reply Brief,16 claims that the PJM Transmission

Owners will use their role in the study process to delay and deny co-location arrangements or

otherwise discriminate against Co-Located Load are baseless and speculative. There simply is no

reason to assume that any PJM Transmission Owner will seek to frustrate the intent of

Commission-accepted tariff provisions.             Likewise, it is illogical to assume that any PJM

Transmission Owners will have an incentive to discriminate against Co-Located Loads in studying



15
          Constellation at 9-12. Constellation’s list of concerns includes rejecting the proposed use of “Point of
Change in Ownership” in the definition of Co-Located Load, imposing deadlines for studies and approvals, and
requiring co-location standards, requirements, guidance, and practices to be filed with the Commission or placed
in the tariff. Id.
16
         Indicated PJM Transmission Owners April 24 Reply Brief at 11.


                                                        7
 such arrangements. As noted above, the primary concern for Transmission Owners in PJM is

system reliability. To the extent Co-Located Load arrangements present no reliability issues, there

is no reason or evidence to suggest that the PJM Transmission Owners will not accommodate their

interconnections.

        B.       Transmission Owner Load Integration Studies Should not be Subject to
                 FERC Filing.

        Constellation claims that the Commission should exercise jurisdiction over load

integration studies conducted by Transmission Owners and direct those load integration studies to

be filed with the Commission.17 This suggestion is meritless. As PJM correctly pointed out in its

April 24 reply brief, the Transmission Owners’ processes for studying the integration of new retail

loads, and identifying associated upgrades, do not inherently implicate the Commission’s

jurisdiction.18 To the contrary, retail load studies have always been subject to state jurisdiction,

and the fact that such studies will be used as one of the inputs into PJM’s process for studying

applications for one of the new transmission services does not provide a sufficient basis for the

Commission to assert jurisdiction over those studies. There is a fundamental distinction between

studying load for purposes of providing retail distribution and energy delivery services, and the

implementation of FERC-jurisdictional interconnection and transmission services, a jurisdictional

line that has long been respected by the Commission.19 Under PJM’s proposed Co-Located Load




17
        Constellation May 11 Answer at 6-7.
18
        PJM April 24 Reply Brief at 34.
19

by Pub. Utils.; Recovery of Stranded Costs by Pub. Utils. and Transmitting Utils., Order No. 888, FERC Stats. &
Regs. ¶ 31,036 (1996) (cross-referenced at 75 FERC ¶ 61,080), on reh’g, Order No. 888-A, FERC Stats. & Regs.
¶ 31,048 (cross-referenced at 78 FERC ¶ 61,220), on reh’g, Order No. 888-B, 81 FERC ¶ 61,248 (1997), on reh’g,
Order No. 888-C, 82 FERC ¶ 61,046 (1998), aff’d in relevant part sub nom., Transmission Access Policy Study
Grp. v. FERC, 225 F.3d 667 (D.C. Cir. 2000), aff’d sub nom., N.Y. v. FERC, 535 U.S. 1 (2002); Standardization
of Generator Interconnection Agreements and Procedures, Order No. 2003, 104 FERC ¶ 61,103 (2003), order on
reh’g, Order No. 2003-A, 106 FERC ¶ 61,220, order on reh’g, Order No. 2003-B, 109 FERC ¶ 61,287 (2004),

                                                      8
 tariff provisions, it is PJM as the Transmission Provider that will make determinations about

whether and to what extent one of the new transmission services can be provided to an applicant.20

These determinations will be transparent, as PJM is required to provide a written explanation with

respect to any denial of service.21

         Moreover, any FERC-jurisdictional transmission facilities needed to accommodate a load

interconnection, be it a Co-Located Load or otherwise, will continue to be subject to the planning

procedures, including the associated stakeholder review and input processes, set forth in PJM’s

Tariff and Operating Agreement, either through the Regional Transmission Expansion Planning

protocols, or the local planning provisions set forth in Attachment M-3. Finally, even with respect

to studies performed with respect to FERC-jurisdictional services, such as generator

interconnection and transmission services, the Commission does not require transmission

providers to file studies, as they are neither service agreements nor rate schedules. To the extent

that a customer has a dispute with the outcome of a particular study, the customer may challenge

that outcome in the context of the Interconnection Agreement or Transmission Service

Agreement process. Similarly, if an Eligible Customer seeking to procure one or more of the

new Co-Located Load transmission services believes that the outcome of PJM’s study process

is flawed, the customer can seek redress through the Commission.




order on reh’g, Order No. 2003-C, 111 FERC ¶ 61,401 (2005), aff’d sub nom. Nat’l Ass’n of Regul. Util. Comm’rs
v. FERC, 475 F.3d 1277 (D.C. Cir. 2007).
20
         PJM February 23 Initial Brief, Illustrative Tariff Sheets at 710.3 (“Following completion of all studies,
Transmission Provider will make the determination, in consultation with the affected PJM Transmission Owner(s),
about whether (and to what level as applicable) Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service or Non-Firm
Contract Demand Transmission Services can be reliably provided for an Application, and if so, what level of
service may be provided.”).
21
         See id. at 710.3 (“If the Transmission Provider determines that only a portion of the Non-Firm Contract
Demand Transmission Service requested by Eligible Customer can be provided reliably, the Transmission Provider
will provide a written explanation of its reasons for partial denial of service.”).


                                                        9
         For these reasons, there is no need or legal basis for FERC to assert jurisdiction over and

require the filing of Transmission Owner load integration studies.

        C.       Objections to the Proposed Grid Reliance Charge are Meritless.

        A few reply briefs take issue with the PJM Transmission Owners’ Grid Reliance Charge

proposal. In general, these briefs claim that the proposed Grid Reliance Charge is unprecedented

and inconsistent with principles of cost causation.22 These objections are misplaced for a number

of reasons.

        The PJM Transmission Owners developed the Grid Reliance Charge partially in response

to Commissioner Chang’s guidance that a just and reasonable replacement rate for the new

transmission services should reflect “some form of minimum transmission service charge, which

would protect other customers against cost shifts resulting from Co-Located Loads that rely upon

the transmission system but do not directly or meaningfully contribute to its costs via transmission

service payments.”23 The PJM Transmission Owners’ proposed Grid Reliance Charge achieves

this goal. As the PJM Transmission Owners explained in their April 24 Reply Brief, the proposed

Grid Reliance Charge is designed to reflect the costs of using the transmission system to deliver

black start and regulation services, as well as the costs of providing the inherent benefits that all

customers, including Contract Demand customers, receive as a result of their synchronization to

and reliance on the grid.24




22
        See, e.g., Constellation at 8; PJM Industrial Customer Organizations and Amtrak at 11-14; Joint Co-
Location Developers at 3-4.
23
        Order, Chang Concurrence at P 9.
24
        Indicated PJM Transmission Owners April 24 Reply Brief at 21.


                                                      10
         In its May 11, 2026 Answer, Constellation presents a handful of criticisms of the PJM

Transmission Owners’ Grid Reliance Charge proposal.25 For example, Constellation’s witness,

Zachary Ming, asserts that the PJM Transmission Owners “fail to address the fundamental

shortcoming of their proposal – a transmission system built only to deliver ancillary services would

be nowhere near as large or expensive as a transmission system built to serve peak demand.”26

Mr. Ming continues to miss the point. The purpose of the Grid Reliance Charge is not merely to

recover the costs of a fictional transmission system built only to deliver ancillary services, but

rather to ensure that Co-Located Load customers pay their fair share of the transmission system as

it exists and the associated benefits that it provides to all interconnected customers, including

essential reliability services, such as frequency support, inertia, voltage stability, fault current

capability, ride-through and protection coordination, and sufficient short-circuit capability.27 The

PJM Transmission Owners’ proposed Grid Reliance Charge does so by calculating the portions of

annual depreciation and operations and maintenance expenses that constitute a reasonable proxy

for the costs of providing those benefits. The Grid Reliance Charge is therefore just and

reasonable.

        In contrast, Constellation’s proposed minimum system replacement proposal28 is not just

and reasonable. The minimum system method is only appropriate for and applicable to

distribution level service. It is entirely inappropriate to apply the minimum system method to



25
         Constellation May 11 Answer at 2 (“The Transmission Owners’ excessive Grid Reliance Charge has no
basis in principle or precedent, while Constellation has proposed a just and reasonable replacement rate the
Commission can readily adopt.”); Id. at 11 (The “Grid Reliance Charge is arbitrary and unmoored from cost
causation principles.”).
26
        Reply Testimony of Zachary Ming at 9:14-16 (“Ming Reply Testimony”).
27
        Indicated PJM Transmission Owners April 24 Reply Brief, Exh. PTO-0005 at 31.
28
        Constellation March 25, 2026 Reply Brief at Attachment 1; Constellation May 11 Answer at 11-13; Ming
Reply Testimony at 11-18.


                                                    11
 calculate a transmission service rate. As Mr. Schafer explains in his further testimony included

as Attachment A to this answer, Mr. Ming continues to fail to account for the fact that the

minimum system approach is only designed as a mechanism to classify portions of certain

distribution plant accounts as either customer- or demand-related.29 It is not, however, used to

determine a revenue requirement, and therefore Mr. Ming’s proposed 6.2% “minimum system”

allocation factor is inappropriate in the context of calculating a transmission service rate.30 Mr.

Ming also continues to base his minimum system analysis on equipment, such as distribution

wood poles, that would not be used for transmission assets, even a hypothetical “minimum”

transmission system that was designed solely to deliver ancillary services.31

       D.       ODEC’s Requests for Clarification are Addressed in PJM’s and the PJM
                Transmission Owners’ Paper Hearing Briefs.

       In its April 24 reply brief, Old Dominion Electric Cooperative (“ODEC”) indicates its

general agreement with the proposals submitted by PJM and the PJM Transmission Owners,

but requests clarification on several items. With respect to the PJM Transmission Owners’

proposal to provide billing credits for revenues associated with the Grid Reliance Charge and

Non-Firm Contract Demand Transmission Service, ODEC requests that the Transmission

Owners confirm the mechanism for providing these credits to customers.32 This issue is

addressed in further detail in the PJM Transmission Owners’ April 24 reply brief, which

includes illustrative tariff language that provides for direct bill credits to customers from PJM

for such revenues.33 ODEC also requests clarification on how regulation and black start service


29
       Reply Testimony of Lance Schafer, Attachment A at 8 (“Schafer Reply Testimony”).
30
       Schafer Reply Testimony at 8-10.
31
       Id. at 10-11.
32
       ODEC at 3.
33
       April 24 Reply Brief, Exh. No. PTO-0006.


                                                  12
 will be charged to Eligible Customers taking service on behalf of Co-Located Load. Based on

PJM’s proposal, the PJM Transmission Owners understand that those charges will be assessed

directly to load-serving entities, in the same manner as they are currently for NITS customers.34

IV.    CONCLUSION

       For the reasons set forth herein, the PJM Transmission Owners respectfully request that

the Commission accept this answer and rule in a manner consistent with the discussion above.

In particular, the Commission should reject attempts to water down requirements to install

sufficient protection systems to ensure Co-Located Load customers do exceed their contractual

commitments. The Commission should also reject arguments to shift costs of Co-Located Load

customers to other ratepayers and accept the PJM Transmission Owners’ proposed Grid

Reliance Charge.

                                                  Respectfully submitted,

 1   II.     BACKGROUND

 2   Q.      What is the background of this proceeding?

 3   A.      On December 18, 2025, the Commission issued its order in PJM Interconnection. L.L.C.,

 4           193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025) (“Order”). In the Order, the Commission found that PJM

 3   Q.       Does the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioner’s Electric Cost

 4            Allocation Manual (“NARUC Manual”) state that the purpose of the minimum

 5            system method is to develop a result that can be applied to a revenue requirement?

 6   A.       No. The NARUC Manual clearly explains that the minimum system method’s purpose is

 7            to classify distribution plant. The NARUC Manual states the following:

 8                    Classifying distribution plant with the minimum-size method assumes that a
 9                    minimum size distribution system can be built to serve the minimum loading
10                    requirements of the customer. The minimum-size method involves determining the
11                    minimum size pole, conductor, cable, transformer, and service that is currently
12                    installed by the utility. Normally, the average book cost for each piece of equipment
13                    determines the price of all installed units. Once determined for each primary plant
14                    account, the minimum size distribution system is classified as customer-related
15                    costs. The demand-related costs for each account are the difference between the
16                    total investment in the account and customer-related costs.12
17
18            The minimum system study, as explained above, serves to classify portions of certain

19            accounts as either customer (i.e., pertaining to the minimum distribution system) or demand

20            related. Mr. Ming’s result of 6.2% merely means that, of the plant accounts included in his

21            study, he determined that 6.2% of the balances are related to a hypothetical minimum

22            system. Therefore, Mr. Ming’s calculation does not represent true revenue requirement for

23            the minimum system represented by that 6.2%.

11   Q.   Please summarize your recommendation regarding Mr. Ming’s testimony?

12   A.   Mr. Ming’s proposal to employ the minimum system method in calculating the Grid

13        Reliance Charge is fundamentally flawed. First, Mr. Ming did not conduct his minimum

14        system study correctly because he included distribution equipment not installed for

15        transmission service. Second, Mr. Ming applies the result of his minimum-system study to

16        the entire transmission revenue requirement, which is contrary to the purpose of the study.

17        Third, the minimum system method only is appropriate for and applicable to distribution-

18        level service. It is entirely inappropriate to apply the minimum system method to calculate

19        a transmission service rate. The Commission should reject Mr. Ming’s proposal and accept

20        the PJM Transmission Owners’ just and reasonable mechanism for determining the Grid

21        Reliance Charge.
